notes: This unit extends Unit 2 with a cost estimate for the future. The supplied 42-slide lecture provides the scope. New executable examples connect the formal guarantees to implementation choices. The cover is conceptual AI-generated artwork and does not represent a graph to solve.
ref: UCLM · Computer Science Degree

title: The route through this unit
body:
Guide the searchCompare UCS, Greedy, A* and Weighted A* on one graph.
Justify the resultDistinguish admissibility, consistency and reopening.
Design a heuristicUse the 8-puzzle, relaxed problems and pattern databases.
Build the lab solverDerive and inspect bounds for geared Loopover.

By the end, a claim of optimality should come with explicit assumptions.
notes: Suggested teaching sequence: three 80-minute sessions. Session one covers priorities and A* traces. Session two covers heuristic properties and construction. Session three applies the theory to Loopover and the Java lab. The HTML supports step-by-step teaching, notes and offline study. The PDF reveals exercise explanations for revision.
sub: Concepts, working examples and laboratory decisions
ref: Adapted from the supplied Unit 3 material

title: Known cost and estimated cost
body:
g(n)

The accumulated cost of the path represented by node n.

h(s)

An estimate of the cheapest remaining cost from state s to a goal.

Two nodes can share a state and h value while having different paths and g values.
notes: Use h(n) as shorthand for h(n.state). A state is a configuration. A node also carries a parent, action and accumulated path cost. The cost g is exact for that particular path, but it is not necessarily the cheapest known cost to the state. Search priorities apply to candidate nodes. This distinction is essential for improvements and reopening.
ref: Adapted from the supplied Unit 3 material

title: The heuristic uses the problem’s cost units
body:
ObjectiveSuitable heuristic unitsA modelling check
Fewest movesEstimated remaining movesOne action must have a clear definition.
Shortest distanceEstimated remaining kilometresGeometric distance needs a valid lower-bound argument.
Minimum travel timeEstimated remaining minutesDistance alone is not a time estimate.

The goal and action model determine what h is allowed to mean.
notes: We assume nonnegative state-based heuristics with h(goal)=0 throughout. A heuristic must refer to the same goal and cost convention as the solver. In Loopover, one coupled row-and-column action costs one. Treating each moved tile as a separate paid action changes the problem. A straight-line travel-time bound would need a justified speed upper bound and compatible movement assumptions.
ref: Original cost-model clarification

title: Three ways to order the frontier
body:
StrategyPriorityWhat it favours
Uniform-cost searchg(n)A cheap path so far.
Greedy best-firsth(n)A state that appears close to a goal.
A*g(n) + h(n)A low estimated total cost via the node.

Setting h = 0 makes A* use the same cost ordering as UCS.
notes: All three can use a priority queue. Changing the priority does not remove the need for successor generation, path reconstruction or repeated-state handling. The exact order among tied priorities depends on a secondary rule. In the main simulator, all strategies use lower h and then insertion order as tie breakers. With h identically zero, the A* and UCS rules coincide.
ref: Adapted from the supplied Unit 3 material

title: Greedy best-first search
body:
f = h

Remove the candidate with the smallest estimate of the remaining cost.

Potential benefit

Useful guidance can lead to a goal after few expansions.

Limitation

The priority ignores the cost already paid.

Even an admissible heuristic does not make Greedy cost-optimal.
notes: The word greedy refers to the choice of frontier priority. It does not imply a particular tie rule or duplicate policy. A low h value says little about how expensive it was to reach that state. The next graph uses a consistent heuristic and still demonstrates a suboptimal Greedy result.
ref: Adapted from the supplied Unit 3 material

title: UCS, Greedy and A* in action
body:
Selection order
Frontier · next first · g / h / priority

Ties: lower h, then insertion order. Goal test on removal. Best-g updates and stale-entry rejection.
notes: Run each strategy from the same initial state. A* selects S,A,B,C,G and returns cost 6. UCS also selects D before the goal and returns cost 6. Greedy selects S,A,G and returns cost 11. Weighted A* is introduced later; w=1 reproduces A*. Selection includes the goal, while the expansion counter excludes it because no goal successors are generated.
ref: Executable original example · No network required

title: Fewer expansions can buy a worse solution
body:
MethodSelection orderExpanded nodesReturned cost
UCSS, D, A, B, C, G56
GreedyS, A, G211
A*S, A, B, C, G46

These are exact counts for this graph and these tie rules, not general speed rankings.
notes: A* avoids the D branch here because g(D)+h(D)=11. Greedy reaches the goal quickly but ignores the high cost of the A-to-G edge. A* still expands A because its admissible heuristic is very optimistic. CPU time would also depend on heuristic evaluation, queue operations and implementation overhead. We report node counts rather than invented timing measurements.
ref: Calculated simulator traces

title: Greedy guarantees depend on the setting
body:
SettingWhat follows
Finite reachable graph with duplicate controlSearch eventually finds a reachable goal or exhausts the frontier.
Infinite search spaceAn infinite sequence of attractive states can prevent progress to a goal.
Unequal route costsThe first goal need not be cheapest, even with an admissible h.

Completeness and cost optimality are separate claims.
notes: The finite-space completeness statement assumes every generated candidate is eventually considered if search does not terminate, finite successor lists and finite heuristic values. The main graph has positive edge costs and explicit best-cost bookkeeping. Infinite-space guarantees for Greedy require more than a helpful-looking heuristic. Avoid unqualified statements that it is always incomplete or always fast.
ref: Adapted from the supplied Unit 3 material

title: A* estimates a complete route through a node
body:
f = g + h

Already paid + estimated remainder.

If h is admissible

f is a lower bound on a solution extending this particular path.

If h is zero

Only the accumulated cost affects the primary order.

The estimate guides which candidate to examine. The returned path still needs validation.
notes: An f value is not necessarily the cost of any actual complete route. It combines an actual prefix with an optimistic suffix. The same state reached via a cheaper prefix receives a smaller f. This is why changing only a state label without replacing its parent and g would be an incorrect update.
ref: Adapted from the supplied Unit 3 material

title: Graph A* with best-cost improvements
body:
best[start] ← 0
push(root(start), priority=h(start))
while frontier is not empty:
    n ← pop_min_f()
    if n.g != best[n.state]: continue
    if goal(n.state): return reconstruct(n)
    for (a, s, cost) in successors(n.state):
        new_g ← n.g + cost
        if new_g < best.get(s, infinity):
            best[s] ← new_g
            push(Node(s, n, a, new_g), new_g + h(s))
return FAILURE

A cheaper path can be queued even when the state was expanded earlier.
notes: This explanatory version uses lazy duplicate entries and allows reopening. A node stores state, parent, action and g; a real implementation may also store depth, h and a sequence number. Because improvements are strict, equal-cost rediscoveries do not create more entries. The stale check precedes the goal test. A state-based deterministic heuristic makes a best-g improvement also an f improvement.
ref: Original pseudocode consistent with the stated A* policy

title: Queue entries and state records have different jobs
body:
best[state]The smallest g discovered so far for that state.
Queue entryAn immutable candidate path with its own g, parent and priority.
Stale entryIts g no longer matches best[state], so it is skipped.
ReopeningA cheaper path reaches a state whose successors were already explored.

The presence of a state in a set does not tell you whether its current path is cheapest.
notes: A priority queue does not usually repair its ordering if a field inside an enqueued object changes. Creating a fresh immutable entry and skipping stale ones is a simple approach. Keep the best-state record separate from the historical node needed for parent reconstruction. Stale entry rejection and reopening are related but distinct mechanisms.
ref: Original implementation clarification

title: Admissibility is a global lower-bound claim
body:
0 ≤ h(s) ≤ h*(s)

h*(s)

The actual minimum remaining cost to any goal.

Consequences

Underestimation is allowed.
Every goal has h = 0.

Checking several examples can disprove admissibility, but cannot establish it for every state.
notes: Our convention includes nonnegativity. Some definitions allow negative admissible values, but that is not needed in this course. If a state has no route to a goal, h* can be treated as infinity. A proof must cover the states on which the heuristic will be used. One state with h greater than a verified solution cost is enough to refute a lower-bound claim.
ref: Adapted from the supplied Unit 3 material

title: Consistency constrains every legal step
body:
h(s) ≤ c(s, a, s′) + h(s′)

Local interpretation

The estimate cannot drop by more than the cost of taking one step.

Goal boundary

Set h(goal) = 0.

The inequality applies to every directed transition.

Consistency plus the goal boundary implies admissibility for states that can reach a goal.
notes: Apply the inequality along any legal path from s to a goal. The heuristic terms telescope, leaving h(s) no greater than that path’s total cost. Taking the cheapest path gives admissibility. The h(goal)=0 boundary is essential: edge inequalities alone also hold for an arbitrary constant positive function, which overestimates at the goal.
ref: Adapted from the supplied Unit 3 material

title: Consistent heuristics make f nondecreasing
body:
f(n′) = g(n) + c(s,a,s′) + h(s′)
≥ g(n) + h(s) = f(n)

Along a generated path

The estimated total cost never falls.

For ordinary A*

A non-stale state removed at minimum f already has its cheapest g.

With a consistent heuristic, an expanded state does not need reopening.
notes: The nondecreasing property refers to f along a path. A consistent graph A* can safely close a state when it is removed, assuming valid cost handling and a fixed goal. An inconsistent admissible heuristic can make f decrease, so early expansion need not settle a state. Weighted A* changes the priority function, so this no-reopening conclusion cannot simply be transferred to it.
ref: Adapted from the supplied Unit 3 material

title: An interactive heuristic check
body:
Edges: S→A:3, S→B:1, B→A:1,
A→G:3, B→G:10.

h(G) = 0. The graph is finite and all its states are shown.
notes: The true remaining costs are S=5, A=3, B=4 and G=0. The initial values 5,0,4,0 are admissible but inconsistent. The failed edges are S→A and B→A. The consistent preset uses 5,3,4,0, which are exact distances. Try increasing h(A) to 4 to violate admissibility. Unlike testing a handful of puzzle states, this checker covers this entire finite graph.
ref: Original complete-graph checker

title: Admissible heuristics may require reopening
body:
Two prefixes to A

S → A costs 3.
S → B → A costs 2.

Fixed heuristic

h(S)=5, h(A)=0,
h(B)=4, h(G)=0.

A is expanded at g = 3 before B reveals its cheaper route.
notes: The heuristic never exceeds the true remaining costs, but it violates consistency. After S is expanded, A has f=3 and B has f=5, so A is removed first. A generates G at cost 6. B is then removed and finds A at cost 2. The solver must consider that improvement to obtain the cost-5 path.
ref: Original admissible-but-inconsistent counterexample

title: Reopening changes the returned answer
body:
Selection order
Frontier · state and g / h / f

Fixed h = {S:5, A:0, B:4, G:0}. The toggle deliberately demonstrates an unsafe closed-set policy.
notes: With reopening enabled, the selected sequence is S,A,B,A,G and the returned path S,B,A,G costs 5. With reopening disabled, the improved route to A is discarded and the returned path S,A,G costs 6. The counterexample is intentionally small so students can verify the guarantee rather than trust an animation. The heuristic is independent of the sliders on the preceding checker.
ref: Executable reopening counterexample

title: The decisive improvement
body:
Eventg(A)Best goal candidateMeaning
A expanded via S3G at cost 6The first route is expensive.
B offers a better route2Still G at cost 6A needs another expansion.
A reopened via B2G at cost 5The goal path improves.

A revised parent chain is part of the improvement.
notes: The best-g map, frontier entry and path reconstruction must agree. Updating only the numeric best cost without propagating a new node can return the wrong path. This table follows the enabled-reopening simulation. It also separates generation of a cheaper goal from selecting the goal at minimum priority.
ref: Calculated reopening trace

title: Why an expensive goal must wait
body:
Candidate goal G

Its heuristic is zero, so f(G)=g(G).

Suppose G is suboptimal

Then g(G) is greater than the optimal cost C*.

Candidate on an optimal path

With admissibility and correct path improvements, some frontier node n satisfies f(n) ≤ C*.

Priority consequence

n is selected before the expensive goal.

The argument needs a correct frontier, an admissible h and appropriate handling of repeats.
notes: This is a proof sketch for the cost of the first selected goal. It relies on maintaining a frontier prefix of an optimal solution, which a no-reopening policy can destroy when h is inconsistent. It does not by itself establish termination on every infinite search space. Completeness requires separate assumptions about branching and costs.
ref: Supplied A* optimality topic · Expanded proof sketch

title: Conditions for A* guarantees
body:
SettingCost guaranteeTermination condition
Tree A* with admissible hFirst selected goal is optimal.For standard completeness: finite branching, finite solution cost and c ≥ ε > 0.
Graph A* with consistent hOptimal without reopening closed states.Finite reachable graph, or the usual positive-cost infinite-space assumptions.
Graph A* with admissible, inconsistent hOptimal with correct improvements and reopening.The same distinction between finite and infinite spaces matters.

Nonnegative costs alone do not rule out an infinite zero-cost search region.
notes: We assume nonnegative h, h(goal)=0 and nonnegative step costs for the cost arguments. A finite reachable graph with finite branching and strict improvements handles zero-cost cycles using repeated-state control. In an infinite space, a positive cost lower bound limits the depth within any finite cost budget. Negative costs invalidate the standard argument. Report failure only after genuine exhaustion, not after a time or memory cap.
ref: Supplied guarantees · Explicit finite/infinite-space assumptions

title: Tie-breaking changes the amount of work
body:
Primary order

Always choose a node with minimum f.

Secondary order

Lower h, then insertion sequence, is the convention used here.

Equal f ⇒ larger g
means smaller h

Those two tie rules are equivalent when f = g + h and the primary f value is equal.

A deterministic rule makes traces reproducible. It does not make every run equally efficient.
notes: The source presents lower h and higher g as separate possibilities. For ordinary A* among exact equal-f ties, they express the same preference. Floating-point comparisons and more complex priorities need explicit handling. Nodes on the f=C* boundary can be treated differently by different tie breakers, affecting counts even with a perfect heuristic. Priority ties must never override a genuinely smaller f.
ref: Adapted from the supplied Unit 3 material

title: Dominance compares lower bounds
body:
ConditionMeaning
h₁ and h₂ are admissibleBoth remain below the same true remaining cost.
h₂(s) ≥ h₁(s) for every stateh₂ dominates h₁ and provides an equally strong or stronger bound.
Evaluation cost also mattersA stronger estimate can take longer to compute.

Dominance alone does not promise a shorter runtime for every implementation and instance.
notes: For consistent A* under comparable conventions, stronger bounds reduce the set of nodes forced below the optimal-cost contour. Boundary ties, reexpansions with inconsistent heuristics, queue overhead and heuristic computation affect actual work. Benchmark under identical tasks and policies. Distinguish a theorem about bounds from a measured runtime claim.
ref: Adapted from the supplied Unit 3 material

title: Combining heuristics with a maximum
body:
h(s) = max(h₁(s), h₂(s))

If both estimates are lower bounds, their maximum remains a lower bound.

Consistency is preserved too

When each component is consistent under the same action costs, their maximum is consistent.

A sum needs a further argument

Two estimates may count the same paid action.

Two heuristics can each equal 1 while only one action is needed. Their sum would overestimate.
notes: For consistency, choose the component i attaining the maximum at s. Then h(s)=h_i(s)≤c+h_i(s′)≤c+max_j h_j(s′). The one-move Loopover example later makes double-counting concrete. This rule concerns fixed state-based heuristics for the same problem and cost convention.
ref: Adapted from the supplied Unit 3 material

Click a numbered tile next to the blank.

Goal: 1 2 3 / 8 □ 4 / 7 6 5.

title: Why Manhattan dominates misplaced tiles
body:
Each misplaced numbered tileContributes at least one unit to Manhattan distance.
One legal blank moveMoves exactly one numbered tile by one grid step.
Lower-bound argumentOne action can reduce the total Manhattan distance by at most one.
Consequenceh_misplaced ≤ h_Manhattan ≤ the optimal number of moves.

The argument relies on this puzzle’s movement and cost rules.
notes: Manhattan distance is the sum of |row−goal_row|+|column−goal_column| over numbered tiles. Each legal move changes that sum by exactly one in this grid puzzle, which also proves consistency. Misplaced count changes by at most one. Scaling Manhattan by two is not generally admissible: one move from the goal gives h=2 but true cost=1. The raw sums cannot be transferred unchanged to coupled Loopover.
ref: Adapted from the supplied Unit 3 material

title: A five-move certificate
body:
MoveBlank directionNumbered tile moved
1Up6
2Up8
3Left2
4Down1
5Right8

Upper bound

The legal five-move sequence reaches the displayed goal.

Lower bound

Initial Manhattan distance is 5.

A cost-5 plan and a cost-5 lower bound together prove that the plan is optimal.
notes: The blank swaps with indices 4,1,0,3,4 in a row-major 0..8 encoding. The sequence transforms 283164705 into 123804765. Independent BFS confirms the shortest length is five. The lower-bound certificate is enough to prove optimality without enumerating all reachable arrangements.
ref: Calculated trace and lower-bound certificate

title: Relaxation removes constraints
body:
01OriginalLegal actions and costs
02RelaxAllow extra possibilities
03SolveFind the relaxed optimum
04UseA lower bound for search

Required relationship

Every concrete plan must have a relaxed counterpart costing no more.

Failure mode

An altered problem that makes actions more expensive need not give a lower bound.

The exact cost of a valid relaxation cannot exceed the original optimum.
notes: Manhattan distance can be understood by relaxing tile interactions so tiles may reach their target positions independently. For cost-preserving abstractions, the mapped solution remains possible. The proof comes from the relationship between plans, not merely from describing the second problem as easier. Computing the relaxed optimum may itself be too expensive unless the relaxation has structure.
ref: Adapted from the supplied Unit 3 material

title: Exact abstract costs can guide concrete search
body:
Concrete state

All tile identities and positions.

Abstract state

Positions of selected tiles. Other identities are ignored.

Stored value

The cheapest abstract cost to the abstract goal.

Lookup

Map the concrete state to its pattern and retrieve the value.

Every concrete action must map to an abstract transition of no greater cost.
notes: The supplied material introduces pattern databases as precomputed distances. For a cost-preserving abstraction, any concrete solution induces an abstract solution, giving a lower bound. The heuristic is exact for the abstract problem, not for the full puzzle. If an abstract edge is assigned the full concrete unit cost, exact abstract goal distances also satisfy the consistency inequality.
ref: Supplied PDB concept · Cost-preserving abstraction

title: A database of distances to the goal
body:
01ProjectChoose pattern and abstract goal
02ReverseGenerate predecessor edges
03SearchBFS for unit costs
04StoreAbstract state to distance

Reverse Dijkstra is the corresponding choice for general nonnegative edge costs.
notes: Distances from the goal equal distances to the goal only when the relevant graph is symmetric. In a directed graph, traverse reversed edges from the goal. Reverse generation may use inverse transformations internally without changing which forward actions are legal. If costs are partitioned into zeros and ones, use an appropriate shortest-path method such as 0–1 BFS. A PDB built in the wrong direction can cease to be a valid goal-distance bound.
ref: Original directed-PDB implementation clarification

title: More tracked tiles require more storage
body:
Pattern tiles kDistinct position assignments 16! / (16−k)!Packed values at 1 byte each
2240240 bytes
443,68042.66 KiB
65,765,7605.50 MiB
8518,918,400494.88 MiB

These are indexing counts and illustrative packed-value sizes, not measured Java memory use.
notes: The table counts placements of k distinct labelled tiles in 16 cells. Reachability and abstraction choices can change which entries are actually stored. A byte per value is possible only if all encoded distances and any sentinels fit. Keys, hash maps, queues and precomputation have additional overhead. The actual two-tile database in this presentation reaches all 240 states and its maximum stored distance is 4.
ref: Calculated permutation counts · Binary memory units

title: Adding patterns requires a cost budget
body:
Safe maximum

max(PDB₁, PDB₂) preserves admissibility when both are lower bounds.

Potentially unsafe sum

Disjoint sets of tile labels can still benefit from the same action.

Cost partitioning

cᵢ(a) ≥ 0
Σᵢ cᵢ(a) ≤ c(a)

Build each PDB using its assigned action costs before summing.

In coupled Loopover, one action moves several tiles, possibly from several patterns.
notes: Additive pattern databases need a justified allocation of each concrete action’s cost. Disjointness of tile labels alone does not prevent double-counting. A concrete plan projects to each pattern, and the sum of its allocated costs cannot exceed its real cost. Therefore the sum of optimal pattern costs remains a lower bound. This is a sufficient construction, not a promise that any arbitrary collection of PDBs is additive.
ref: Felner, Korf & Hanan (2004), Additive Pattern Database Heuristics

title: The coupled action is the cost unit
body:
00010203040506070809101112131415
StateA full 4 × 4 board of distinct tiles 00–15.
Action r c +Shift row r right, then column c down.
Action r c −Shift row r left, then column c up.
CostOne per complete coupled action.

Column c refers to the fixed column index after the row phase.
notes: This matches Units 1 and 2 and the laboratory rules in the supplied material. The board is toroidal and has no blank. There are 4×4×2=32 action labels. Intermediate row-only boards are not one-step successors. We now derive heuristics specifically for this action model.
ref: Supplied geared Loopover model

title: One action moves seven distinct tiles
body:
Support of the transformation

Four row positions and four column positions share one cell.

4 + 4 − 1 = 7

Total elementary displacement

The row phase moves four tiles one step. The column phase moves four tiles one step.

4 + 4 = 8

One tile participates in both phases. Distinct tiles and unit displacements are different counts.
notes: The composed permutation changes only positions in the selected row or column. Its support has seven distinct cells. One tile experiences both a horizontal and a vertical shift; six other tiles experience one shift each. These facts provide upper bounds on how much one paid action can repair. The argument applies to either sign and all row/column choices.
ref: Original derivation from the supplied action rule

title: Raw tile counts can overestimate the cost
body:
One move before the goal

01060300040510070809141112130215

Apply 02+

The row-right then column-down action reaches the ordered goal.

Before the action

Misplaced tiles m = 7
Toroidal distance sum D = 8
True remaining cost = 1

Neither raw m nor raw D is admissible under this coupled unit-cost model.
notes: The state is 01060300040510070809141112130215. It is a predecessor of the goal under action 02+, obtained by undoing column 2 first and row 0 second. It is not the state formed by applying 02+ to the goal. The distinction matters because the inverse transformation reverses phase order. This single counterexample disproves two tempting raw-count heuristics.
ref: Calculated one-action counterexample

title: A lower bound from misplaced tiles
body:
hₘ(s) = ⌈m(s) / 7⌉
At most seven repairsOne action affects seven distinct tile positions.
Any solution of length LCan repair at most 7L currently misplaced tiles in total.
Lower boundm(s) ≤ 7L, so every solution needs at least ⌈m/7⌉ actions.

The ceiling matters because the action count is an integer.
notes: A move may also displace correct tiles, which only makes the actual solution longer. For consistency, m(s)≤7+m(s′) across a legal unit-cost edge. Taking ceilings gives h_m(s)≤1+h_m(s′). At the goal m=0. Thus the bound is both admissible and consistent, not just plausible on selected boards.
ref: Original proof for geared 4 × 4 Loopover

title: A lower bound from toroidal distance
body:
D(s) = Σ tiles [min(|Δr|, 4−|Δr|)
+ min(|Δc|, 4−|Δc|)]
hᴅ(s) = ⌈D(s) / 8⌉

Wraparound distance

Row 0 and row 3 are one step apart on a four-cell ring.

Per-action progress

The eight elementary displacements can reduce D by at most eight.

D(s) ≤ 8 + D(s′) also gives consistency of the rounded bound.
notes: For each tile, compare its current coordinates with the coordinates of its goal cell. A unit ring movement changes its toroidal Manhattan distance by at most one. Sum over the four row movements and four column movements. Even the tile moved in both phases contributes at most two units of reduction. Dividing by eight converts tile-step distance into a lower bound measured in coupled actions.
ref: Original toroidal-distance proof for the supplied rules

title: A combined bound with a clear proof
body:
h_basic = max(hₘ, hᴅ)

Both components are admissible and consistent.

Adding a pattern database

h = max(hₘ, hᴅ, h_PDB)

The same properties hold for a cost-preserving PDB.

Using hₘ + hᴅ would already overestimate on the one-move example: 1 + 1 > 1.
notes: There is no need to assert that one analytical bound always dominates the other. The maximum is safe regardless. A PDB may improve the maximum in some states and contribute nothing in others. The live examples show both possibilities. The combined heuristic still might be weak for difficult instances; admissibility is a correctness property, not a speed guarantee.
ref: Original combination of the derived bounds

title: A live Loopover heuristic laboratory
body: Crimson tiles 00 and 01 form the pattern.
notes: The two-tile PDB tracks the positions of 00 and 01 and is built by reverse BFS over all 240 ordered distinct-position states. Every abstract forward edge costs one. The UI displays raw m and D, their rounded lower bounds, the exact abstract PDB value and the combined maximum. Undo restores the previous whole board from history; it does not assume that changing the action sign undoes a move. The full puzzle is not solved automatically.
ref: Executable 240-state PDB · Derived analytical bounds

title: A pattern detects what counts miss
body:
12010200040506070809101103131415

Only three tiles are misplaced

m = 3, D = 4.
hₘ = 1 and hᴅ = 1.

The two-tile abstraction says more

h_PDB = 2.

A matching solution

00+ followed by 00− reaches the goal.

A two-step lower bound plus a two-step solution proves the optimum is 2.
notes: The concrete state is 12010200040506070809101103131415. The PDB only tracks tiles 00 and 01 but accounts for their shared action effects. The tracked pair needs an abstract route of at least two actions. Opposite signs in the same row-then-column phase order do not generally cancel; the example is also a useful test against that implementation mistake.
ref: Calculated two-action certificate using the exact abstract PDB

title: Reverse generation must reverse phase order
body:
Forward 02+

1. Row 0 right.
2. Column 2 down.

Predecessor transformation

1. Column 2 up.
2. Row 0 left.

The predecessor operation is for reverse search. It does not introduce a new legal forward action.
notes: For a composed action T=C∘R, the inverse is R⁻¹∘C⁻¹. Applying it to a target board executes C⁻¹ first and then R⁻¹. The forward action 02− instead executes row-left first and column-up second, so it is generally different. The PDB builder iterates the actual inverse transformation of each forward label to construct reversed abstract edges.

title: The Weighted A* cost bound
body:
C_returned ≤ w C*

For fixed w ≥ 1 with an admissible nonnegative h and h(goal)=0.

Implementation conditions

Nonnegative action costs, minimum-priority removal, valid best-g improvements and reopening when required.

Termination

A finite reachable graph suffices here. Infinite spaces need further completeness assumptions.

An arbitrary overestimating heuristic does not inherit this weight bound.
notes: A frontier node on an optimal path has g+w h≤w(g+h*)=w C*, since g≥0. Correct improvements preserve such a prefix until the goal is selected. The selected goal has h=0, so its cost cannot exceed that candidate priority. Do not transfer the ordinary consistent-A* no-reopening rule to Weighted A* without another argument. This is a cost bound, not a prediction of the actual error.
ref: Hansen & Zhou (2007), Anytime Heuristic Search · Bound explanation

title: IDA* deepens an f threshold
body:
01Initializethreshold = h(start)
02TraverseDepth-first within g + h ≤ threshold
03RecordSmallest exceeded f value
04RepeatUse that value as the next threshold

Memory advantage

Store the current path and limited traversal information.

Work repeated

The search regenerates states across thresholds.

IDS deepens a depth bound. IDA* deepens a cost-estimate bound.
notes: With an admissible heuristic and standard positive-cost, finite-branching assumptions, IDA* can find optimal solutions while using much less memory than A*. Use path-cycle checks and stop when a threshold traversal finds a goal. The next threshold is the smallest exceeded f, not necessarily the previous threshold plus one, especially with noninteger costs. Implementation details affect repeated-state overhead.
ref: Adapted from the supplied Unit 3 material

title: Other ways to limit search memory
body:
MethodMain ideaWhat it gives up or needs
RBFSFollow the most promising path and retain backed-up alternatives.May regenerate forgotten subtrees.
SMA*Use a memory budget and forget poor leaves while backing up their values.Guarantees depend on enough memory for relevant solution paths.
Full A*Retain frontier candidates and cost records.Memory may grow too large before the goal is selected.

A memory limit is a reported search outcome, not proof that a puzzle is unsolvable.
notes: These are conceptual extensions from the source lecture, not additional required lab implementations. Avoid saying that SMA* is complete for every arbitrary memory cap. A solver cannot retain a solution path longer than its available representation budget. Record resource exhaustion separately from failure after full frontier exhaustion.

title: A useful benchmark isolates the heuristic

Same task setIdentical initial states, goals, action costs and successor order.
Same correctness policyBest-g updates, reopening, stopping rule and tie breaker.
Search effortGenerated nodes, expansions, reexpansions and peak frontier.
Actual costWall time, heuristic time, peak memory and returned solution cost.

Count the PDB build cost and storage, and state whether they are amortized across many runs.
notes: Use fixed input instances and reproducible seeds. Separate a cold run that constructs the PDB from warm runs using an existing database. Report all resource limits. Compare returned cost with a proven optimum only where one is available; otherwise call it a reference bound. Never label a timeout as a failed proof of reachability. The presentation gives exact toy counts but makes no large-scale performance claims.

title: The A* implementation contract
body:
Immutable queue recordsChanging an enqueued priority in place can invalidate the heap order.
State-keyed best costEquality identifies configurations, independent of parent or depth.
Heuristic on the childCompute h from the resulting state and the correct goal.
Revised pathA cheaper g comes with the corresponding parent and action.
Honest terminationSolution, frontier exhausted, or an explicit resource limit.

The implementation and the proof must describe the same algorithm.
notes: For Java PriorityQueue, a new entry plus stale-entry skipping is a straightforward alternative to decrease-key. The comparator should use safe numeric comparisons instead of subtracting values that may overflow. This is general design guidance, not an API-version-specific code sample. Keep h deterministic for a fixed problem unless the algorithm explicitly supports changing heuristic values.
ref: Adapted from the supplied Unit 3 material

title: Workshop: defend or reject a heuristic
body:
Proposed heuristicQuestion to justify
h=0 on the entire state spaceWhat does it guarantee, and how much guidance does it provide?
2 × Manhattan for the unit-cost 8-puzzleCan one nearby state refute admissibility?
Raw misplaced tiles for coupled LoopoverHow many tiles can one paid action repair?
Sum of two full-cost disjoint-tile PDBsCan one action help both patterns?

For a rejection, provide a counterexample. For acceptance, state a general argument.
notes: Suggested duration: six minutes in pairs. Require students to identify the action and cost model before classifying the proposal. A heuristic being cheap, informative or random is not by itself evidence of admissibility. Ask stronger students whether a randomly selected fixed value bounded by a proven h would be admissible; it would, although consistency would not follow automatically.
ref: Expanded activity based on the supplied admissibility questions

title: Heuristic workshop: reasoned answers
body:
ProposalConclusion and evidence
h=0Admissible and consistent for nonnegative costs; A* becomes UCS.
2 × ManhattanNot generally admissible: one move away gives 2 instead of 1.
Raw misplaced Loopover tilesNot admissible here: the verified one-move state has 7 misplaced tiles.
Sum of full-cost PDBsNot guaranteed: an action can be counted in both estimates. Use a maximum or prove a cost partition.

“Admissible” always refers to a particular problem, goal and cost model.
notes: Distinguish proof of invalidity from lack of a proof. The first two counterexamples explicitly exceed a known optimal cost. The PDB answer explains why the proposed general guarantee fails, rather than asserting that every possible sum fails on every state. Revisit the one-move Loopover board, where multiple independent-looking estimates each account for the same single action.
ref: Worked solutions to the heuristic activity

title: Six checks for optimal A*
body:
01

What does g describe?

The exact cost of this candidate path, not necessarily the cheapest path to its state.
02

What does admissibility require?

A lower bound on remaining cost for every relevant state.
03

What does consistency add?

An inequality for every legal edge, with h(goal)=0.
04

When might A* reopen a state?

When an inconsistent heuristic lets it expand a state before a cheaper path arrives.
05

Why can a raw Loopover count fail?

One coupled unit-cost action moves seven distinct tiles.
06

When can PDB values be added?

When a valid cost allocation prevents counting the same action cost more than once.
notes: Use these questions as short retrieval practice. Follow an answer with the corresponding graph, bound proof or one-move counterexample. The HTML hides explanations until requested. The PDF shows all six explanations for self-study.
ref: Original learning check
